Based on my research, here is a thorough overview of the **neuroscience debates about free will**, organized by core questions, pivotal studies, and arguments on both sides.

---

## 1. What Is the Core Question?

The central issue: Does conscious intention play any genuine causal role in our decisions, or are all choices generated unconsciously by the brain before we become aware of deciding? If the latter, does that mean "free will" is an illusion?

---

## 2. The Pioneer Study: Libet (1983)

In their landmark paper **Libet et al., *Brain* 106:623–664 (1983)**, Benjamin Libet and colleagues asked participants to flex their wrists "whenever they felt like it" while EEG recorded brain activity. Participants also used an oscilloscope clock to report the exact moment (**W-time**) they had the conscious intention to act.

**Finding:** A negative-going EEG signal called the **readiness potential (RP)** began on average **~550 ms before the movement** and **~350–400 ms before the W-time** (Libet et al., 1983). Libet concluded that "cerebral initiation even of a spontaneous voluntary act … can and usually does begin unconsciously" (cited from **Kinsbourne, *Conscious Intention and Human Action*, Brain & Cognition 147 (2021)**). This seemed to undermine the ordinary notion of free will: conscious will appears *after* the brain has already started initiating action.

---

## 3. Later Brain-Prediction Studies

Several follow-up studies claimed to push the "unconscious decision" finding further:

### Soon et al., *Nature Neuroscience* (2008)
Chrstian K. Soon and John-Dylan Haynes used fMRI with multivariate pattern classification to show that brain activity in **medial prefrontal and anterior frontopolar cortex** could predict which of two button-press choices a participant would make **up to ~7 seconds before conscious awareness** (citation: **"Unconscious determinants of free decisions in the human brain," *Nature Neuroscience* 11:543–545, 2008**; URL retrieved: https://www.nature.com/articles/nn.2112.pdf).

### Haynes & Reeke (2013) / Morelli et al. (2013)
Morelli et al., **PNAS 110:694–699 (2013)**, extended this further: the outcome of a free decision to **add or subtract numbers** could be decoded from neural activity in medial prefrontal and parietal cortex **~4 seconds before subjects reported consciously making their choice**. "These choice-predictive signals co-occurred with the so-called default mode brain activity pattern… Our results suggest that unconscious preparation of free choices is not restricted to motor preparation" (from PNAS article retrieved at https://www.pnas.org/doi/abs/10.1073/pnas.1212218110).

These studies are frequently cited by those arguing free will is illusory (e.g., **Sam Harris** popularly) — brain "decides" before consciousness knows it.

---

## 4. Major Criticisms of the Libet/Readiness-Potential Paradigm

Multiple lines of criticism have been raised against interpreting RP as "the brain deciding":

### a) The RP may be an artifact of averaging
**Kinsbourne (2021)** reviewed this literature in "**Conscious intention and human action: Review of the rise and fall of the readiness potential and Libet's clock,** *Brain & Cognition* 147 (2021)" and pointed out that **recent observations suggest the RP may only be an "artifact of averaging"** — the buildup pattern disappears in single-trial analyses, meaning it does not necessarily reflect a genuine decision process on any given trial.

### b) Timing ambiguities: W-time is unreliable
The introspective report of *when* one first became consciously aware of intending to move has been criticized as unreliable. **Van den Brink et al. ("(Non)-experiencing the intention to move...," PubMed 37127128, 2023)** showed that W-time is affected by the experimental procedures themselves: "participants who had prior experience reporting the M-time provided significantly earlier W-time" — and even naive participants differentiated W-time from M-time introspectively. They concluded "the relatedness of both the RP and the W-time to the movement initiation processes should not be assumed as a priori."

### c) The RP does not unequivocally indicate motor intention onset
**Muller, Vorburger, & Koenig (2013)** ("Does the brain 'initiate' freely willed processes? A philosophy of science critique of Libet-type experiments," *European Journal for Philosophy of Science* 3:207–235) argued from a detailed methodological analysis that **Libet's experiment does not show that the readiness potential signals the initiation of a free choice** — they raised issues about what exactly is being measured, how EEG averages work, and what counts as a "decision."

### d) Stochastic fluctuation models
The **"stochastic decision model" (SDM)** offers an alternative to Libet's interpretation: rather than RP being a "decision signal," it may simply be **the accumulation of ongoing random/noisy neuronal fluctuations** over time. In this view, the actual decision happens later — when accumulated noisy signal plus any imperative reaches a threshold — not at RP onset (from **Klein et al., PubMed 37901069, 2023**: we clarified that "the deterministic component of the model is quantitatively the dominant input into the accumulator" and the role of random fluctuations has been overstated in the literature).

---
